Broadway enters the spring of 2026 with a remarkably diverse lineup that balances groundbreaking new works with beloved revivals and long-running favorites. This month's top-rated shows achieve an impressive average critic score of 83/100, reflecting a theater season firing on all cylinders.

Leading the pack is **Hamilton**, which continues to prove why it remains Broadway's most revolutionary musical nearly eleven years after its debut. Lin-Manuel Rodríguez's hip-hop retelling of American history still earns the highest critical acclaim with a 90/100 rating, demonstrating that true innovation has lasting power.

The season's most exciting newcomer is **Maybe Happy Ending**, a robot love story that critics are calling one of Broadway's most original musicals in years. With an 85/100 score, this charming production proves that audiences still hunger for fresh narratives that push theatrical boundaries. Meanwhile, **Oh, Mary!**—Cole Escola's absurdist take on Mary Todd Lincoln as a boozy cabaret dreamer—continues to pack houses with its riotous comedy, earning an 84/100 rating.

Classic spectacles remain strong, with **The Lion King** and **The Book of Mormon** both scoring 83/100, while the timely **Ragtime** revival resonates with contemporary audiences. **Hadestown** continues its folk-opera enchantment, and **Harry Potter and the Cursed Child** dazzles with theatrical magic, even as critics debate its narrative merits.

Whether you're drawn to hip-hop history lessons, romantic robots, or mythological folk operas, March 2026 offers something exceptional for every theatergoer. Use the detailed reviews and ratings below to find your next unforgettable Broadway experience.

best-broadway-plays.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays: March 2026

As Broadway heads into the spring of 2026, the play landscape offers an eclectic mix ranging from audacious historical revisionism to wizarding spectacle. With an average critic score of 75 out of 100 across our featured productions, this month's selections lean heavily on technical showmanship and unconventional storytelling.

Leading the pack is **Oh, Mary!**, Cole Escola's absurdist farce that reimagines Mary Todd Lincoln as a cabaret-obsessed, cocktail-swilling narcissist. With 84 out of 100 from 33 reviews, the production earns consistent raves for its riotous comedy and fearless irreverence toward American history. It stands as March's critical favorite, proving that bold comedic risks can pay off handsomely.

**Harry Potter and the Cursed Child** continues its strong run with an 82 out of 100 rating from 69 reviews. Critics remain divided on the narrative—some find the time-turner plot convoluted—but there's near-universal acclaim for the production's spectacular stagecraft and magical illusions that continue to push theatrical boundaries.

Further down the list, **Stranger Things: The First Shadow** brings Netflix's hit series to the stage with impressive special effects and technical wizardry, though its three-hour runtime and overstuffed prequel narrative leave some critics wanting tighter storytelling. Meanwhile, **Every Brilliant Thing** rounds out the selection, though with only one review logged, it remains too early to draw definitive conclusions.

Whether you're drawn to irreverent comedy, magical spectacle, or sci-fi stagecraft, March's play offerings prioritize visual ambition and genre-bending approaches—check individual show pages for full reviews, ticket information, and performance schedules.

best-broadway-shows-for-kids.intro:

**The Lion King** leads the field as the highest-rated option, earning an 83/100 from critics who continue to celebrate Julie Taymor's innovative puppetry and costume design nearly three decades into its historic run. The production remains a benchmark for theatrical artistry that appeals across generations.

Close behind, **Harry Potter and the Cursed Child** scores 82/100, impressing critics with its technical wizardry and stagecraft illusions, though reviewers note the narrative doesn't always match the visual spectacle. The two-part play brings J.K. Rowling's magical world to life in ways that particularly resonate with young fans of the book series.

The remaining selections—**Aladdin**, **& Juliet**, **Wicked**, and **MJ The Musical**—each score between 70-71/100, representing solid if somewhat polarizing options. When selecting a show for your family, consider both the critic scores and your child's specific interests—whether they're drawn to classic Disney tales, magical adventures, pop music, or biographical spectacles. Each production offers a different gateway into the theatrical experience.

At 77/100 across 26 reviews, the show proves that intimate storytelling can hold its own against larger-scale productions.

The revival of **Chess** generates more mixed reactions. While critics consistently praise the ABBA score and the vocal performances from Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit, and the ensemble, opinions diverge on the production as a whole, resulting in a 65/100 average across 29 reviews.

With an overall average critic score of 73/100 across the featured shows, March presents a solid if not spectacular lineup. The range—from sweeping historical epic to intimate contemporary comedy—offers theatergoers genuine variety in tone and scale. Whether you're drawn to the grand ambitions of classic revivals or the understated charm of new voices, this month's Broadway landscape has options worth exploring.

best-broadway-shows-2020.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows from 2020

As we look back in March 2026 at the Broadway productions that premiered six years ago, the class of 2020 represents a season dramatically cut short by the pandemic—making the shows that did open all the more historically significant. These five productions, which debuted before Broadway's unprecedented shutdown, offer a fascinating snapshot of theater at a pivotal moment.

The standout among these survivors is **Les Misérables**, earning an 83/100 from critics for its grittier reboot at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre. This reimagined production breathes new life into the beloved musical, though its darker approach doesn't win over every traditionalist. Close behind is **A Soldier's Play**, scoring 78/100 for its powerful Broadway debut—a long-overdue arrival for Charles Fuller's Pulitzer-winning drama that critics agree remains urgently relevant in its examination of race and justice within the military.

The season shows notable diversity in form and ambition, from Laura Linney's solo turn in **My Name is Lucy Barton** (71/100) to the boulevard comedy of **Grand Horizons** (71/100), elevated by veterans Jane Alexander and James Cromwell. Perhaps most divisive is Ivo van Hove's radical **West Side Story** reimagining (68/100), which polarizes audiences with its bold video design and visceral staging choices.

With an average critic score of 74/100 across these five productions, the 2020 season demonstrates the range of theatrical voices that were just finding their footing before the industry's historic pause. For theatergoers interested in understanding Broadway's evolution through one of its most tumultuous periods, these productions offer essential viewing and context for where American theater has traveled since.

Meanwhile, **The Lehman Trilogy** stands as an epic achievement, with critics lauding its sweeping examination of American capitalism through extraordinary performances and masterful direction.

More intimate productions like **Is This a Room** and **Lackawanna Blues** demonstrate the power of minimalist storytelling, with the former transforming a verbatim FBI transcript into gripping theater and the latter showcasing Ruben Santiago-Hudson's virtuosic solo performance.

From Antoinette Chinonye Nwandu's **Pass Over**, which appropriately served as Broadway's reopening production, to crowd-pleasers like **SIX** and the enduring **Phantom of the Opera**, the 2021 season offered something for every theatergoer. Whether you're seeking experimental boundary-pushing work or reimagined classics, these productions continue to define what made Broadway's return so vital.
